title: Cargo of the Brig Aurora v. United States (1813)
shortTitle: Cargo of the Brig Aurora v. United States (1813)
summary: Congress could make revival of a trade restriction depend on the President’s determination that a foreign nation had stopped violating American neutral commerce.

sections.Parties: The cargo claimant appealed a federal condemnation of goods imported aboard the brig Aurora. The United States sought forfeiture under the revived restrictions on trade with Great Britain.
sections.Material Facts: Congress’s 1809 nonintercourse legislation prohibited specified imports from Britain and France and made unlawfully imported goods forfeitable. After that legislation expired, the May 1810 statute provided that if either nation stopped violating American neutral commerce, the President would proclaim the fact and restrictions would revive against the other nation. President Madison proclaimed France’s compliance in November 1810. The Aurora sailed from Liverpool in December and reached New Orleans in February 1811; its cargo was seized. The Court also determined that the cargo was not American property eligible for a later exemption.
sections.Procedural History: The district court for Orleans condemned the cargo. On the claimant’s appeal, the Supreme Court rejected the objections to the revival and timing of the import restrictions. The excerpt supplies the condemnation appeal and the Court’s resolution of its material questions, but omits the opinion’s closing decretal language.
sections.Issue: Could Congress constitutionally make revival of an expired statutory restriction depend on a presidential proclamation, and did the revived restriction operate before the cargo arrived?
sections.Holding: Congress could enact a conditional revival. Revival gave the prohibition the force it had when it expired; the operative prohibition began on February 2, 1811, rather than waiting for a new May 20 date.
sections.Reasoning: The claimant argued that giving a proclamation the effect of activating law transferred legislative power. The government answered that Congress itself prescribed both the legal consequence and the factual condition; the proclamation supplied evidence that the condition existed. The Court found no sufficient reason to deny Congress discretion to revive its law expressly or conditionally. It separately read revival to restore the existing prohibition’s immediate force, because suspending operation until May would conflict with the instruction that the revived provisions have full force. The decision supports conditional legislation, while its brief discussion leaves later courts to explain how much evaluative discretion a factual trigger may contain.
